## Packages

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
```

## Data wrangling

![](https://github.com/allisonhorst/stats-illustrations/raw/main/rstats-artwork/dplyr_wrangling.png){fig-alt="Cartoon of fuzzy monsters wrangling data with dplyr." width="55%"}

Real-world data is usually messy.
Once it's in a tidy "shape",
we only need a few dplyr functions for most of our work.

::: {.aside}
Artwork by Allison Horst (CC BY 4.0).
:::

## The Palmer penguins

This dataset has 344 penguins of 3 species,
collected from 3 islands near Palmer Station, Antarctica.
It's been built into R since version 4.5.
We'll convert it into a tibble so it prints nicely.

```{r}
penguins <- as_tibble(penguins)
penguins
```

## `select()`: choose columns

```{r}
select(penguins, species, bill_len, body_mass)
```

```{r}
select(penguins, starts_with("bill"))
```

## `filter()`: choose rows

```{r}
filter(penguins, flipper_len > 190)
```

```{r}
filter(penguins, flipper_len > 190 & species == "Chinstrap")
```

## `mutate()`: add or change columns

Body mass is in grams,
so let's add a column with the mass in kilograms.

```{r}
mutate(penguins, body_mass_kg = body_mass / 1000)
```

`mutate()` gives back a new data frame and doesn't change `penguins`.
If we want to keep the result, we need to assign it (`<-`) to a variable.

## Doing many steps at once

We can save each step as its own object,

```{r}
penguins_1 <- mutate(penguins, body_mass_kg = body_mass / 1000)
penguins_2 <- filter(penguins_1, flipper_len > 190)
penguins_3 <- select(penguins_2, species, flipper_len, body_mass_kg)
```

or we can nest the function calls,
but then we have to read them from the inside out.

```{r}
penguins_nested <- select(
  filter(mutate(penguins, body_mass_kg = body_mass / 1000), flipper_len > 190),
  species, flipper_len, body_mass_kg
)
```

## The pipe, `|>`

The pipe takes whatever is on its left
and passes it in as the first argument of the function on its right.
We can read each `|>` as "and then".

```{r}
penguins |>
  mutate(body_mass_kg = body_mass / 1000) |>
  filter(flipper_len > 190) |>
  select(species, flipper_len, body_mass_kg)
```

## `group_by()` and `summarize()`

`group_by()` splits the data into groups,
and `summarize()` calculates a single value for each group.

```{r}
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarize(avg_body_mass = mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE))
```

We need `na.rm = TRUE` to skip the missing values.
Otherwise, a single `NA` makes the whole mean `NA`.

## How many values are missing?

```{r}
penguins |>
  summarize(n = n(), missing_body_mass = sum(is.na(body_mass)))
```

```{r}
penguins |>
  count(species, island)
```

## Visualization: ask a question, then answer it

![](https://github.com/allisonhorst/stats-illustrations/raw/main/rstats-artwork/ggplot2_exploratory.png){fig-alt="Cartoon of fuzzy monsters exploring data with ggplot2." width="45%"}

When we make a plot,
we're trying to answer a question about our data,
and a good plot answers it clearly.

::: {.aside}
Artwork by Allison Horst (CC BY 4.0).
:::

## ggplot2: three parts

Every ggplot2 plot is built from the same parts:

1. Aesthetic mappings, which map columns to visual properties
   (`x`, `y`, `colour`, `fill`)
2. Geometric objects (geoms), which say how to draw them
   (`geom_point()`, `geom_histogram()`, `geom_bar()`)
3. Scales and labels for the axes, colours, and titles

We add each layer with `+`.

## Scatter plot: two quantitative variables

Is a penguin's body mass related to its flipper length?

```{r}
#| warning: false
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_point()
```

## Add colour and labels

```{r}
#| warning: false
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    colour = "Species"
  )
```

## Histogram: one quantitative variable

```{r}
#| warning: false
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass, fill = species)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 250, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Number of penguins", fill = "Species")
```

## Bar plot: counts of a categorical variable

```{r}
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = island, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Island", y = "Number of penguins", fill = "Species")
```

## Rules of thumb

- Answer one question per plot
- Label axes, with units
- Use colourblind-friendly palettes
- Avoid pie charts, 3D, and tables of numbers when a plot will do
